W01-D1-01.altText: LAiDIES STOP editorial card. Large text reads: “Specificity is not secret syntax. It is a useful brief.” Supporting line: “Specificity—not secret syntax—gives AI a better chance of producing something you can use.”
W01-D1-01.fullText: STOP: Tell it what useful looks like. Opening: Specificity is not secret syntax. It is a useful brief. Alternative openings: Your AI prompt has “the usual” energy at a café that has never met you. / A vague prompt is “fold in the cheese” for a machine. Lesson: Specificity—not secret syntax—gives AI a better chance of producing something you can use. Instagram text: Prompting is not coding. It is briefing a smart new hire who has never met your director, your project or your office politics. Give it the audience, context, tone, constraints and definition of good. LinkedIn text: Prompting is not coding. It is delegation. If the output sounds generic, inspect the brief before blaming the tool: who is this for, what do they care about, what should success look like, and what should the draft leave out? Safety note: Do not imply specificity guarantees factual accuracy.

W01-D1-02.altText: LAiDIES TEACH editorial card. Large text reads: “AI cannot read your mind, your meeting notes or your office politics.” Supporting line: “A useful brief names audience, goal, context, tone, constraints, length and exclusions.”
W01-D1-02.fullText: TEACH: Brief the smart new hire. Opening: AI cannot read your mind, your meeting notes or your office politics. Alternative openings: The tool is new here. Give it the first-week briefing. / Before you rewrite the output, rewrite the assignment. Lesson: A useful brief names audience, goal, context, tone, constraints, length and exclusions. Instagram text: Before you ask AI to make something better, define better. Audience. Goal. Context. Tone. Constraints. Length. What not to include. That is the brief. LinkedIn text: The practical prompt checklist I use is the same checklist I would use with a capable new teammate: audience, goal, context, tone, constraints, length and exclusions. Better delegation is more reusable than memorizing a magic prompt formula. Safety note: Teach the checklist, not a universal formula.

W01-D1-04.fullText: JOIN: Which briefing detail goes missing?. Opening: Which part of the brief do you skip when you are rushing? Alternative openings: Be honest: audience, context, tone or constraints—which one disappears first? / What does your AI have to guess most often? Instagram text: Poll: when the prompt goes vague, what usually went missing—audience, context, tone or constraints? LinkedIn text: When an AI draft comes back generic, which briefing detail was most likely missing: audience, context, tone or constraints? No confidential examples—just the pattern. Safety note: Do not solicit private prompts or workplace documents.

W01-D1-05.fullText: VISIT / RETURN: Read the full specificity lesson. Opening: Your next better prompt starts with a better brief. Alternative openings: Same tool. Same Tuesday. W01-D2-01.altText: LAiDIES STOP editorial card. Large text reads: “AI can be helpful and wrong in the same answer.” Supporting line: “Readers learn that polished tone and factual reliability are separate judgments.”
W01-D2-01.fullText: STOP: Helpful and wrong. Opening: AI can be helpful and wrong in the same answer. Alternative openings: The dangerous sentence is the one that looks ready to leave your laptop. / Full Regina George confidence is not a source. Lesson: Readers learn that polished tone and factual reliability are separate judgments. Instagram text: The output can be useful, polished and wrong in the same paragraph. Tone is not a receipt. LinkedIn text: The most dangerous AI error is rarely obvious nonsense. It is the normal-looking sentence sitting beside two supported ones. Treat fluency and evidence as separate checks. Safety note: Avoid fear-based “AI lies” framing.

W01-D2-02.altText: LAiDIES TEACH editorial card. Large text reads: “Before you fact-check everything, decide what kind of sentence you are holding.” Supporting line: “Classifying output as draft, claim or inference focuses verification effort.”
W01-D2-02.fullText: TEACH: Draft or claim?. Opening: Before you fact-check everything, decide what kind of sentence you are holding. Alternative openings: Drafting help and factual claims need different checks. / Not every sentence needs a trial. Some definitely need receipts. Lesson: Classifying output as draft, claim or inference focuses verification effort. Instagram text: DRAFT: edit for usefulness. CLAIM: verify. INFERENCE: label and challenge. The first move is knowing which one you are holding. LinkedIn text: A practical review shortcut: classify the output. Drafting language needs editing. Factual claims need sources. Inferences need assumptions made visible. The categories keep verification proportionate. Safety note: High-stakes work still requires domain review.

W01-D2-03.altText: LAiDIES SAVE / SEND editorial card. Large text reads: “Names. Dates. Numbers. Quotes. Links. Check these first.” Supporting line: “A five-item check gives readers an immediately reusable verification habit.”
W01-D2-03.fullText: SAVE / SEND: The receipt pass. Opening: Names. Dates. Numbers. Quotes. Links. Check these first. Alternative openings: Five tiny details most likely to embarrass a polished draft. / Save the receipt pass before the answer borrows your name. Lesson: A five-item check gives readers an immediately reusable verification habit. Instagram text: Before your name goes on it: check every NAME, DATE, NUMBER, QUOTE and LINK. Then check whether the source actually supports the sentence. LinkedIn text: My fastest first verification pass is boring on purpose: names, dates, numbers, quotes and links. Each can look plausible while being wrong, stale or attached to the wrong context. Safety note: A checklist is a first pass, not full assurance.

W01-D3-01.altText: LAiDIES STOP editorial card. Large text reads: “You do not need a 40-hour AI course before you open the tab.” Supporting line: “A smaller first step reduces shame and makes action plausible.”
W01-D3-01.fullText: STOP: You do not need the 40-hour course. Opening: You do not need a 40-hour AI course before you open the tab. Alternative openings: Ten useful minutes beats waiting for a mythical free weekend. / AI fluency can start with one low-risk Tuesday task. Lesson: A smaller first step reduces shame and makes action plausible. Instagram text: Start with one low-risk task. Compare the result. Keep your judgment. That is a real beginning. LinkedIn text: People are being told to “get good at AI” as if a free weekend is about to appear. A more credible start is one low-risk task, ten useful minutes and a deliberate review of what helped. Safety note: Do not minimize organization-specific AI policies.

W01-D3-02.altText: LAiDIES TEACH editorial card. Large text reads: “Generative AI is not Google in a blazer.” Supporting line: “Readers gain a simple, bounded mental model for generative AI.”
W01-D3-02.fullText: TEACH: Not Google in a blazer. Opening: Generative AI is not Google in a blazer. Alternative openings: Search retrieves. Generative AI produces a new draft. / The first useful distinction: finding versus generating. Lesson: Readers gain a simple, bounded mental model for generative AI. Instagram text: Search helps you find existing pages. Generative AI produces a new response from patterns in its training and your context. New output still needs review. LinkedIn text: A useful first distinction: search retrieves existing information; generative AI produces a new response. That is why the result can help draft, summarize or compare—and why it still needs judgment. Safety note: Keep the model accurate; do not claim search never generates.

W01-D4-01.altText: LAiDIES STOP editorial card. Large text reads: “Does the draft sound useful—or like a LinkedIn quote printed on a throw pillow?” Supporting line: “A vivid quality test helps readers recognize generic output.”
W01-D4-01.fullText: STOP: The LinkedIn throw pillow test. Opening: Does the draft sound useful—or like a LinkedIn quote printed on a throw pillow? Alternative openings: Generic output has a very specific throw-pillow energy. / If the paragraph could belong to every company, it belongs to none. Lesson: A vivid quality test helps readers recognize generic output. Instagram text: If the paragraph could be sent by every company to every audience, the brief probably left the tool guessing. LinkedIn text: A slightly dangerous LinkedIn test: could this AI draft be printed on a motivational throw pillow without changing a word? If yes, the assignment probably needs a real audience and a concrete decision. Safety note: Critique generic output, not people using LinkedIn.

W01-D4-02.altText: LAiDIES TEACH editorial card. Large text reads: “Same tool. Same task. One useful variable changed.” Supporting line: “A before/after demonstration makes the mechanism visible.”
W01-D4-02.fullText: TEACH: Same task, better context. Opening: Same tool. Same task. One useful variable changed. Alternative openings: The second prompt worked because the audience finally existed. / Context is the difference between a paragraph and your paragraph. Lesson: A before/after demonstration makes the mechanism visible. Instagram text: Vague: summarize this policy. Better: name the six readers, their two-minute window, what changed, what action they need and what background to omit. LinkedIn text: A better prompt does not need ornamental syntax. It needs the reader, their priorities, the decision, the constraints and the exclusions. The improvement is visible because the assignment changed. Safety note: Examples must stay synthetic and low risk.

W01-D5-01.altText: LAiDIES STOP editorial card. Large text reads: “A perfectly polished answer can still be in the wrong room.” Supporting line: “Relevance is exposed as a separate quality dimension from plausibility.”
W01-D5-01.fullText: STOP: She does not even go here. Opening: A perfectly polished answer can still be in the wrong room. Alternative openings: That is a U.S. HR answer in a Canadian workplace. / Useful draft. Wrong company, country, date or decision. Lesson: Relevance is exposed as a separate quality dimension from plausibility. Instagram text: The answer may be correct somewhere. Your job is to check whether it belongs to this company, country, customer, tool, date and decision. LinkedIn text: A common AI failure is not fabrication; it is misplaced relevance. The answer may be true for another jurisdiction, product version or organization. “Correct somewhere” is not the same as usable here. Safety note: No legal or HR advice.

W01-D5-02.altText: LAiDIES TEACH editorial card. Large text reads: “Before you ask “is it true?”, ask “is it true here?”” Supporting line: “Readers learn to bind a claim to its actual scope.”
W01-D5-02.fullText: TEACH: The relevance check. Opening: Before you ask “is it true?”, ask “is it true here?” Alternative openings: Truth has a company, country, product and date. / Context is part of correctness. Lesson: Readers learn to bind a claim to its actual scope. Instagram text: Check: our company? our country? this customer? this tool/version? this date? this decision? Context is not decoration; it is part of correctness. LinkedIn text: A source can be real and the answer still unusable. Bind the claim to company, jurisdiction, customer, product version, date and decision before it enters the final work. Safety note: Do not imply the framework replaces expert review.

W01-D6-01.fullText: STOP: AI was not invented last Tuesday. Opening: AI was not invented by guys in hoodies last Tuesday. Alternative openings: The history of computing has women’s names all over it. / The newest AI headline sits on nearly two centuries of work. Lesson: The audience receives a corrective historical frame without a novelty myth. Use it to remember the AI idea. / Nostalgia is useful when it carries the lesson. Lesson: The audience understands the distinctive LAiDIES teaching proposition. Instagram text: The reference is not decoration. It earns its place when it makes the technical idea easier to understand, remember and use. LinkedIn text: LAiDIES uses familiar cultural references as retrieval cues, not wallpaper. The test is simple: if you remove the reference, does the explanation become harder to understand or remember? If not, the reference was decoration. Safety note: No unlicensed clips or long quotations.
